Contrast with the bride's state by nature (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Is 1:6</reference>) her state by grace (<reference osisRef="Song.4.1-Song.4.7">So 4:1-7</reference>), "perfect through His comeliness put upon her" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.14">Eze 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.3">Joh 15:3</reference>). The praise of Jesus Christ, unlike that of the world, hurts not, but edifies; as His, not ours, is the glory (<reference osisRef="John.5.44">Joh 5:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.4.10">Re 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.11">11</reference>). Seven features of beauty are specified (<reference osisRef="Song.4.1-Song.4.5">So 4:1-5</reference>) ("lips" and "speech" are but one feature, <reference osisRef="Song.4.3">So 4:3</reference>), the number for perfection. To each of these is attached a comparison from nature: the resemblances consist not so much in outward likeness, as in the combined sensations of delight produced by contemplating these natural objects.<div eID="gen12973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doves'--</hi>the large melting eye of the Syrian dove appears especially beautiful amid the foliage of its native groves: so the bride's "eyes within her locks" (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.44">Lu 7:44</reference>). Maurer for "locks," has "veil"; but locks suit the connection better: so the Hebrew is translated (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.2">Is 47:2</reference>). The dove was the only bird counted "clean" for sacrifice. Once the heart was "the cage of every unclean and hateful bird." Grace makes the change.<div eID="gen12974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyes--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.6.22">Mt 6:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>; contrast <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28">Mt 5:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.16">1Jo 2:16</reference>). Chaste and guileless ("harmless," <reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">Mt 10:16</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="John.1.47">Joh 1:47</reference>). John the Baptist, historically, was the "turtledove" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.12">So 2:12</reference>), with eye directed to the coming Bridegroom: his Nazarite unshorn hair answers to "locks" (<reference osisRef="John.1.29">Joh 1:29</reference>, 36).<div eID="gen12975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hair ... goats--</hi>The hair of goats in the East is fine like silk. As long hair is her glory, and marks her subjection to man (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.6-1Cor.11.15">1Co 11:6-15</reference>), so the Nazarite's hair marked his subjection and separation unto God. (Compare <reference osisRef="Judg.16.17">Jud 16:17</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.17">2Co 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1Pe 2:9</reference>). Jesus Christ cares for the minutest concerns of His saints (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.30">Mt 10:30</reference>).<div eID="gen12976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12977" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appear from--</hi>literally, "that lie down from"; lying along the hillside, they seem to hang from it: a picture of the bride's hanging tresses.<div eID="gen12977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gilead--</hi>beyond Jordan: there stood "the heap of witness" (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.48">Ge 31:48</reference>). <div eID="gen12978" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 4 So 4:1-16 . 1. Contrast with the bride's state by nature ( Is 1:6 ) her state by grace ( So 4:1-7 ), "perfect through His comeliness put upon her" ( Eze 16:14 ; Joh 15:3 ). The praise of Jesus Christ, unlike that of the world, hurts not, but edifies; as His, not ours, is the glory ( Joh 5:44 ; Re 4:10 , 11 ). Seven features of beauty are specified ( So 4:1-5 ) ("lips" and "speech" are but one feature, So 4:3 ), the number for perfection. To each of these is attached a comparison from nature: the resemblances consist not so much in outward likeness, as in the combined sensations of delight produced by contemplating these natural objects. doves'-- the large melting eye of the Syrian dove appears especially beautiful amid the foliage of its native groves: so the bride's "eyes within her locks" ( Lu 7:44 ). Maurer for "locks," has "veil"; but locks suit the connection better: so the Hebrew is translated ( Is 47:2 ). The dove was the only bird counted "clean" for sacrifice. Once the heart was "the cage of every unclean and hateful bird." Grace makes the change. eyes-- ( Mt 6:22 ; Ep 1:18 ; contrast Mt 5:28 ; Ep 4:18 ; 1Jo 2:16 ). Chaste and guileless ("harmless," Mt 10:16 , Margin; Joh 1:47 ). John the Baptist, historically, was the "turtledove" ( So 2:12 ), with eye directed to the coming Bridegroom: his Nazarite unshorn hair answers to "locks" ( Joh 1:29 , 36). hair ... goats-- The hair of goats in the East is fine like silk. As long hair is her glory, and marks her subjection to man ( 1Co 11:6-15 ), so the Nazarite's hair marked his subjection and separation unto God. (Compare Jud 16:17 , with 2Co 6:17 ; Tit 2:14 ; 1Pe 2:9 ). Jesus Christ cares for the minutest concerns of His saints ( Mt 10:30 ). appear from-- literally, "that lie down from"; lying along the hillside, they seem to hang from it: a picture of the bride's hanging tresses. Gilead-- beyond Jordan: there stood "the heap of witness" ( Ge 31:48 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8238"/><div sID="gen12979" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8238"/><hi type="bold">2. even shorn--</hi>the Hebrew is translated (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.25">1Ki 6:25</reference>), "of one size"; so the point of comparison to teeth is their symmetry of form; as in "came up from the washing," the spotless whiteness; and in "twins," the exact correspondence of the upper and lower teeth: and in "none barren," none wanting, none without its fellow. Faith is the tooth with which we eat the living bread (<reference osisRef="John.6.35">Joh 6:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.54">54</reference>). Contrast the teeth of sinners (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Psa 57:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.14">Pr 30:14</reference>); also their end (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.7">Psa 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.30">Mt 25:30</reference>). Faith leads the flock to the washing (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zec 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1Co 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen12979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none ... barren--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.8">2Pe 1:8</reference>). He who is begotten of God begets instrumentally other sons of God. <div eID="gen12980" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8240"/><div sID="gen12986" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8240"/><hi type="bold">4. neck--</hi>stately: in beautiful contrast to the blushing temples (<reference osisRef="Song.4.3">So 4:3</reference>); not "stiff" (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.4">Is 48:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>), as that of unbroken nature; nor "stretched forth" wantonly (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Is 3:16</reference>); nor burdened with the legal yoke (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.14">La 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.10">Ac 15:10</reference>); but erect in gospel freedom (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.2">Is 52:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12987" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tower of David--</hi>probably on Zion. He was a man of war, preparatory to the reign of Solomon, the king of peace. So warfare in the case of Jesus Christ and His saints precedes the coming rest. Each soul won from Satan by Him is a trophy gracing the bride (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.22">Lu 11:22</reference>); (each hangs on Him, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.23">Is 22:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.24">24</reference>); also each victory of her faith. As shields adorn a temple's walls (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.11">Eze 27:11</reference>), so necklaces hang on the bride's neck (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.30">Jud 5:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.16">1Ki 10:16</reference>). <div eID="gen12987" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8241"/><div sID="gen12988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8241"/><hi type="bold">5. breasts--</hi>The bust is left open in Eastern dress. The breastplate of the high priest was made of "two" pieces, folded one on the other, in which were the Urim and Thummim (lights and perfection). "Faith and love" are the double breastplate (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">1Th 5:8</reference>), answering to "hearing the word" and "keeping it," in a similar connection with breasts (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.27">Lu 12:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.28">28</reference>).<div eID="gen12988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">roes--</hi>He reciprocates her praise (<reference osisRef="Song.2.9">So 2:9</reference>). Emblem of love and satisfaction (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">Pr 5:19</reference>).<div eID="gen12989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12990" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.23.2">Psa 23:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among the lilies--</hi>shrinking from thorns of strife, worldliness, and ungodliness (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.7">Mt 13:7</reference>). Roes feed among, not on the lilies: where these grow, there is moisture producing green pasturage. The lilies represent her white dress (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">Psa 45:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Re 19:8</reference>). <div eID="gen12991" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8242"/><div sID="gen12992" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8242"/>6. Historically, the hill of frankincense is Calvary, where, "through the eternal Spirit He offered Himself"; the mountain of myrrh is His embalmment (<reference osisRef="John.19.39">Joh 19:39</reference>) till the resurrection "daybreak." The third Canticle occupies the one cloudless day of His presence on earth, beginning from the night (<reference osisRef="Song.2.17">So 2:17</reference>) and ending with the night of His departure (<reference osisRef="Song.4.6">So 4:6</reference>). His promise is almost exactly in the words of her prayer (<reference osisRef="Song.2.17">So 2:17</reference>), (the same Holy Ghost breathing in Jesus Christ and His praying people), with the difference that she then looked for His visible coming. He now tells her that when He shall have gone from sight, He still is to be met with spiritually in prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.16">Psa 68:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Mt 28:20</reference>), until the everlasting day break, when we shall see face to face (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.10">1Co 13:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen12992" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8248"/><div sID="gen13012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8248"/>12. The Hebrew has no "is." Here she is distinct from the garden (<reference osisRef="Song.5.1">So 5:1</reference>), yet identified with it (<reference osisRef="Song.4.16">So 4:16</reference>) as being one with Him in His sufferings. Historically the Paradise, into which the soul of Jesus Christ entered at death; and the tomb of Joseph, in which His body was laid amid "myrrh," &c. (<reference osisRef="Song.4.6">So 4:6</reference>), situated in a nicely kept garden (compare "gardener," <reference osisRef="John.20.15">Joh 20:15</reference>); "sealed" with a stone (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.66">Mt 27:66</reference>); in which it resembles "wells" in the East (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.3">Ge 29:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.8">8</reference>). It was in a garden of light Adam fell; in a garden of darkness, Gethsemane, and chiefly that of the tomb, the second Adam retrieved us. Spiritually the garden is the gospel kingdom of heaven. Here all is ripe; previously (<reference osisRef="Song.2.13">So 2:13</reference>) it was "the tender grape." The garden is His, though He calls the plants hers (<reference osisRef="Song.4.13">So 4:13</reference>) by His gift (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Is 61:3</reference>, end).<div eID="gen13012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spring ... fountain--</hi>Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="John.4.10">Joh 4:10</reference>) sealed, while He was in the sealed tomb: it poured forth its full tide on Pentecost (<reference osisRef="John.7.37-John.7.39">Joh 7:37-39</reference>). Still He is a sealed fountain until the Holy Ghost opens it to one (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1Co 12:3</reference>). The Church also is "a garden enclosed" (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Is 5:1</reference>, &c.). Contrast <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9-Ps.80.12">Psa 80:9-12</reference>. So "a spring" (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">Is 27:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">58:11</reference>); "sealed" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.30">Ep 4:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>). As wives in the East are secluded from public gaze, so believers (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.3">Psa 83:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">Col 3:3</reference>). Contrast the open streams which "pass away" (<reference osisRef="Job.6.15-Job.6.18">Job 6:15-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.17">2Pe 2:17</reference>). <div eID="gen13013" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8252"/><div sID="gen13021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8252"/><hi type="bold">16. Awake--</hi>literally, "arise." All besides is ready; one thing alone is wanted--the breath of God. This follows rightly after His death (<reference osisRef="Song.6.12">So 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.1-Acts.2.4">Ac 2:1-4</reference>). It is His call to the Spirit to come (<reference osisRef="John.14.16">Joh 14:16</reference>); in <reference osisRef="John.3.8">Joh 3:8</reference>, compared to "the wind"; quickening (<reference osisRef="John.6.63">Joh 6:63</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.9">Eze 27:9</reference>). Saints offer the same prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.6">Psa 85:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.2">Ha 3:2</reference>). The north wind "awakes," or arises strongly, namely, the Holy Ghost as a reprover (<reference osisRef="John.16.8-John.16.11">Joh 16:8-11</reference>); the south wind "comes" gently, namely, the Holy Ghost as the comforter (<reference osisRef="John.14.16">Joh 14:16</reference>). The west wind brings rain from the sea (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.44">1Ki 18:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.45">45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.54">Lu 12:54</reference>). entries.content_plain: 16. Awake-- literally, "arise." All besides is ready; one thing alone is wanted--the breath of God. This follows rightly after His death ( So 6:12 ; Ac 2:1-4 ). It is His call to the Spirit to come ( Joh 14:16 ); in Joh 3:8 , compared to "the wind"; quickening ( Joh 6:63 ; Eze 27:9 ). Saints offer the same prayer ( Psa 85:6 ; Ha 3:2 ). The north wind "awakes," or arises strongly, namely, the Holy Ghost as a reprover ( Joh 16:8-11 ); the south wind "comes" gently, namely, the Holy Ghost as the comforter ( Joh 14:16 ). The west wind brings rain from the sea ( 1Ki 18:44 , 45 ; Lu 12:54 ). The east wind is tempestuous ( Job 27:21 ; Is 27:8 ) and withering ( Ge 41:23 ). These, therefore, are not wanted; but first the north wind clearing the air ( Job 37:22 ; Pr 25:23 ), and then the warm south wind ( Job 37:17 ); so the Holy Ghost first clearing away mists of gloom, error, unbelief, sin, which intercept the light of Jesus Christ, then infusing spiritual warmth ( 2Co 4:6 ), causing the graces to exhale their odor. Let my beloved, &c.-- the bride's reply. The fruit was now at length ripe; the last passover, which He had so desired, is come ( Lu 22:7 , 15, 16 , 18 ), the only occasion in which He took charge of the preparations. his-- answering to Jesus Christ's "My." She owns that the garden is His, and the fruits in her, which she does not in false humility deny ( Psa 66:16 ; Ac 21:19 ; 1Co 15:10 ) are His ( Joh 15:8 ; Php 1:11 ).
